name: Magnetic Field Model
what: This subtopic introduces the field model as a way of describing magnetism. It covers how magnetic fields are represented using field lines, the properties of those field lines, the concepts of dipoles and monopoles, and the difference between uniform and non-uniform fields.
why: Understanding the field model is the foundation for analysing all magnetic phenomena in this topic. It allows you to predict directions of forces, interpret diagrams, and connect magnetism with electricity and gravity using a consistent framework.

items.title: I can describe magnetism using a field model
items.what: A magnetic field is a region around a magnet where a magnetic force can be experienced. The field model describes this invisible influence using field lines that show direction and relative strength.
items.why: Using a field model allows us to describe and predict magnetic effects without needing to see the actual forces directly. This same model applies to gravity and electric fields, making it a unifying idea in physics.
items.example: Iron filings sprinkled near a bar magnet align themselves along the field lines, making the invisible magnetic field visible as curved lines running from the north pole to the south pole outside the magnet.

items.title: I can apply Faraday's three rules for magnetic field lines
items.what: Faraday's rules state that: field lines are continuous loops leaving the north pole and entering the south pole; field lines never cross or intersect each other; and the closeness of field lines indicates the strength of the field.
items.why: These rules make magnetic field diagrams consistent and meaningful. Without them, diagrams could be drawn in contradictory ways that don't reflect real physical behaviour.
items.example: Near the poles of a bar magnet where field lines are drawn close together, the field is strong (about 0.5 T for a school magnet). At a point further away where field lines are spread apart, the field is much weaker.

items.title: I can explain why magnetic fields are dipole fields and compare this to electric and gravitational fields
items.what: A magnetic dipole has two poles (north and south) that always appear together. No isolated magnetic pole (monopole) has ever been observed. Gravity has only monopoles (mass), while electricity has both monopoles (isolated charges) and dipoles (paired charges).
items.why: Understanding the difference between monopoles and dipoles explains why you can never separate the north and south poles of a magnet, and why breaking a magnet always produces two smaller complete magnets.
items.example: If you break a bar magnet in half, each piece becomes a weaker magnet with its own north and south pole. You cannot isolate a single north pole, unlike an electric charge which can exist alone.

items.title: I can identify and describe magnetic fields as uniform or non-uniform, and as static or changing
items.what: A uniform magnetic field has the same strength and direction at every point; it is shown by parallel, evenly spaced field lines. A non-uniform field varies in strength or direction across space. A static field does not change over time.
items.why: Many calculations in this topic assume a uniform magnetic field. Recognising when a field is uniform (such as between the poles of a U-shaped magnet) allows you to apply formulas confidently.
items.example: The region directly between the poles of a U-shaped magnet produces a nearly uniform static field, represented by parallel equally spaced horizontal lines. The field around a single bar magnet is non-uniform because field lines curve and become less dense further from the poles.

items.title: I can use the arrow convention to represent magnetic fields going into or out of the page
items.what: When a magnetic field is directed into the page, it is represented by a cross (✕), like the tail of an arrow moving away. When it is directed out of the page, it is represented by a dot (•), like the tip of an arrow coming towards you.
items.why: Physics problems often involve three-dimensional field directions that must be shown on a flat page. This convention provides a clear, universal way to communicate field direction in diagrams.
items.example: In a diagram showing an electron moving to the right through a magnetic field directed into the page, you would draw a row of crosses (✕) filling the region to represent the field pointing away from you.

items.title: I can describe the attractive and repulsive interactions between magnetic poles, and compare these to electric and gravitational interactions
items.what: Unlike magnetic poles attract (north attracts south) and like poles repel (north repels north). Electric charges also attract and repel in the same pattern. Gravitational masses, however, only ever attract each other — there is no gravitational repulsion.
items.why: Comparing these three field types reveals that gravity is unique in having only one type of source (mass), while magnetism and electricity involve two types. This comparison is a key part of the study design.
items.example: Two bar magnets with north poles facing each other will push apart. Two bar magnets with a north pole facing a south pole will pull together. Two masses will always pull together, regardless of what they are made of.
